transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, it's... I mean, I'm here because I just need someone to understand what's been happening at work. I drive a transit bus, you know, and lately, it's just been impossible to ignore what dispatch is doing. They've been tracking my route changes, but not in the normal way, not like how they usually monitor the lines. It's through the computer system, and I can see the little discrepancies, the way the GPS updates lag exactly when I'm at certain intersections. And then there are the comments on the radio. Just these little, seemingly innocent remarks from dispatch, but they're not innocent. They're coded. I know they're tracking me specifically. And I've tried to talk to people about it, you know, maybe bring it up casually, and they always say, "Oh, it's just normal oversight, they track everyone, it's compliance." But it's not. I can tell. I can just feel it. And it's not just dispatch, either. It's the other drivers. Certain ones, anyway. I see the way they look at me in the breakroom, the way they get on their radios right after I pull out of the depot. They're reporting on me, feeding information back to compliance. It's this whole coordinated thing, and no one else seems to see it, but it's happening every single shift, and it's just... it's exhausting trying to do my job when I know they're all watching my every move like that.
Have you been hearing voices when no one is actually there?

Voices? Like... people who aren't there? No. No, definitely not. I mean, I hear voices all day, but they're real. They're on the radio. You know, when you're driving one of those heavy-duty transit buses, the two-way radio is just constantly going off, just crackling all shift. So I hear dispatch, and I hear the other drivers on the frequency, but it's not... it's not imaginary. It's actual people. 

I know their voices. I know exactly when it's Marcus on the mic, or when it's Sarah from compliance. Sometimes they try to keep it really low, or they'll clip their sentences short so it just sounds like radio interference or static, but my hearing is perfectly fine. Actually, it's probably sharper than most people's because you have to be so hyper-aware when you're navigating a forty-foot vehicle through downtown traffic, keeping an eye on the mirrors, the passengers, the GPS lagging, and listening to the dispatch codes all at the exact same time. You can't miss a single detail. So, if you're asking if I'm imagining people speaking to me out of thin air in an empty room, no, absolutely not. The voices I hear are the people at the depot who are coordinating all of this, and they are very, very real.
Lately, have you been needing much less sleep than usual and still feeling full of energy?

Less sleep? No, definitely not. I mean, full of energy? I wish. Honestly, if anything, I'm just completely exhausted all the time. You have to understand, driving a heavy transit bus takes a massive physical toll on you, your back, your shoulders, not to mention the mental part of it right now with everything going on with dispatch. 

I usually work the early shift, which means my alarm goes off at exactly 3:15 AM. I have this whole strict routine because I have to be at the depot by 4:00 AM to do my pre-trip inspections—you know, checking the air brakes, walking the perimeter of the bus, logging into the terminal system before I even pull out of the yard. And to do all that safely, and to keep my guard up, I absolutely have to get my seven or eight hours of sleep. I mean, I force myself to go to bed by 7:30 PM every night. I draw the blackout curtains, I make sure the room is completely quiet, I even make this specific chamomile tea to help me wind down, because if I don't get that sleep, my reaction times drop, and I just can't afford that. 

Not with downtown traffic, and definitely not with compliance watching my every move. I have to be sharp to catch those little discrepancies I was telling you about. So no, I'm not running on empty and feeling great about it or bouncing off the walls. By the time I finish my route, pull the bus back into the yard, and hand over my logs, I am just completely drained. It takes every ounce of energy I have just to stay one step ahead of them during the day. So, yeah, I definitely need my sleep, probably more now than I ever did before just to cope with how tiring the whole situation is.
Have you had any recent seizures, head injuries, or other neurological problems?

Seizures? Head injuries? No. No, nothing like that. I mean, I know what a concussion feels like—when I was, gosh, maybe twelve, I fell off my bike going down this really steep hill near my parents' house and hit my head on the curb. I had to go to the hospital, and they did all these tests, shining the little light in my eyes, asking me what day it was, all that. I remember the headache lasted for like a week, and I couldn't look at bright lights. But recently? No. 

And as for neurological problems, I mean, if I had something wrong with my brain like that, I wouldn't be able to drive the bus. The Department of Transportation is incredibly strict about medical clearances for commercial drivers. We have to do these physicals, the DOT physicals, every two years, and they check everything. They check your vision, your hearing, your blood pressure, and they specifically ask about any history of seizures or fainting spells. If you even hint that you've had a dizzy spell, they can pull your medical card right then and there, and you're grounded. You can't even get behind the wheel of a shuttle van, let alone a forty-foot transit bus. 

So, I have to be completely healthy in that regard. My last physical was... let's see, it was about eight months ago, I think? Yeah, eight months ago, with Dr. Aris at the occupational health clinic downtown. He signed off on everything. My reflexes were perfect, my balance was fine. I mean, you need perfect coordination to maneuver those buses, especially when you're making those tight right turns at intersections where people park too close to the corner, or when you have to suddenly brake because a pedestrian steps out without looking. You can't have any kind of neurological delay or whatever you want to call it. 

So, physically, my brain is fine. It's just... it's the stress of what's happening at work that's getting to me, not some medical condition in my head. I haven't hit my head, I haven't passed out, no seizures, nothing like that. My brain works perfectly fine, which is exactly why I'm able to pick up on all these things that dispatch is doing. If there was something wrong with my head, I probably wouldn't even notice the GPS lags or the codes they use on the radio. But I do notice them, because I'm sharp. So, no, no head injuries or anything like that.
How long has this been going on?

How long? Well, let me think... it hasn't been forever, but it feels like it's been a really long time because of how intense it is every single day. I'd say... it's been building for about eight months now. Yeah, exactly eight months. 

I know that for sure because that's when they put me in the temporary dispatch lead role. It was supposed to be a great opportunity, you know? They told me I had the seniority and the perfect safety record, so they brought me inside the depot to cover for Marcus when he went on paternity leave. I thought it was just going to be logging routes, managing the break schedules, and handling the two-way radio for the downtown grid. But the second I sat in that chair, in that little glass office overlooking the yard, I started noticing things. 

At first, it was just small stuff—like how the dispatch codes they were logging didn't match the actual GPS locations of the buses. I'd see a bus marked as being on 4th and Elm, but the live feed showed them sitting idle behind the old warehouse district. And when I tried to bring it up to Sarah in compliance, she just brushed it off, said it was a system glitch. But you don't get system glitches that specific, not every single day, and not always with the same three drivers. 

So, I started keeping my own log. I'd sit there during my breaks, cross-referencing the radio chatter with the transit maps. And that's when I realized they were using the radio static—the clipping I told you about—to coordinate whatever it is they're doing. When Marcus came back from leave and they put me back behind the wheel, I thought maybe it would stop, or maybe I just wouldn't be as exposed to it. But it actually got worse, because now I was out there on the routes, and I could hear them talking about me on the frequency. 

So yeah, eight months. Eight months of having to be constantly on high alert, checking my mirrors, listening to every single crackle on that radio, just waiting for them to slip up so I can finally prove what's going on. It's exhausting, it really is, but I can't let my guard down, not even for a second, not since I was in that dispatch office and saw how the whole thing actually works from the inside.
Aside from dealing with this situation at work, have you been having trouble keeping up with your normal daily activities?

Trouble keeping up? I mean... I guess, if I'm being completely honest, yeah. It’s hard to admit because I’ve always been such an organized person, you know? But it’s just taking up so much of my mental space. 

At work, I’ve actually fallen really far behind on my route reports. We have to file these detailed end-of-shift logs—passenger counts, delay justifications, mileage—and lately, I just sit in the breakroom staring at the paperwork because my mind is just replaying everything I heard on the radio that day. And when I do have to use the radio to coordinate with the other buses at the downtown transfer hubs, my instructions have gotten confusing enough that the other drivers actually complain. They’ve complained to management! They say they don't know what I'm talking about, but that's just because I'm trying to factor in the weird codes dispatch is using, and they aren't paying attention to the big picture like I am. But still, it's causing problems.

And then at home... gosh, my poor husband. He's been an absolute saint through all of this, but I know it's not fair to him. I used to be the one who handled everything for us. I'd meal prep on Sundays, making sure we had healthy lunches for the week so we wouldn't waste money eating out, I'd keep the calendar... but now? I walk through the front door and I am just so depleted from tracking everything at the depot that I can't even think. My husband has had to completely take over all the meals. He's doing the cooking, the grocery shopping, everything. 

And it's not just the food, it's the phone calls, too. Like calling the landlord about the maintenance stuff, or paying the utility bills... I just can't bring myself to pick up the phone or look at a schedule because I'm so burnt out. He's basically had to take over all the basic planning for our lives right now because I’m just... I'm just not keeping up. I try, I really do, but there's only so much bandwidth a person has when they're dealing with what I'm dealing with all day.
Have you noticed yourself becoming much less interested in socializing with other people than you used to be?

Socializing? Yeah... yeah, I really have. Which is so strange for me, because I used to be the one who pulled everyone together, you know? Like, we have this recreational softball team at the depot—the Transit Titans, we call ourselves—and I used to be the one who hosted everyone after our Thursday night games. I’d set up the patio, have the cooler full of drinks, make these little barbecue sliders... I loved it. I loved having the team over and just laughing and unwinding. But lately? The thought of having the softball team over just makes me want to lock the door and hide. If anyone even hints at hanging out after a shift, I just make up an excuse. I don't want to talk to them, I don't want to entertain... I just don't want them around. 

And it's not just the people from work, either. I've been in a community choir for three years now. I sing alto. I used to look forward to our Tuesday night rehearsals all week long, just the feeling of all those voices coming together, you know? But I just... I don't feel like singing with the choir anymore. I haven't gone in weeks. The director actually texted me a couple of times to see if I was sick, and I couldn't even bring myself to text him back. I just look at the phone and feel nothing. The idea of standing on those risers and making small talk during the water breaks just feels completely impossible. 

It all just ties back into what I was saying before about home. It’s this heavy, empty feeling. Most days after my shift, I come through the front door, I drop my keys in the little ceramic bowl, and I just sit at the kitchen table. I still open my planner—out of habit, I guess, because I used to color-code everything in it—but I just sit there with the planner open in front of me. I stare at the blank pages. I know I need to do things. I know I should get up and start dinner, or make those calls to the landlord, or do the laundry, or literally anything else... but I just can't make myself start. I can't make myself care enough to move. I just sit there at the table, sometimes for an hour or more, just staring at the paper until my husband comes in and asks if I'm okay. I just don't want to do any of it anymore.
Before these past eight months, had you ever had a similar experience of feeling that people were tracking you or communicating in coded ways?

Before these past eight months? No... no, never. Honestly, if you had told me a year ago that I’d be sitting here talking to a doctor about radio clipping and GPS discrepancies, I would have thought you were joking. 

Before I took that dispatch cover for Marcus, my life was just... completely normal. I drove the Route 42 loop—that’s the one that goes past the community college and winds down through the arts district. It’s a really great route, actually. You get a lot of students, a lot of regulars who take the same bus at the exact same time every morning, so you really get to know people. I knew my passengers, I knew my schedule, and I never, ever felt like anyone was watching me or tracking me. I mean, sure, the transit supervisors do their routine checks, but that’s just standard procedure, you know? That’s just them standing on the corner with a clipboard making sure we’re hitting our time points at the major stops so the whole grid doesn't fall behind. 

I never had any reason to suspect anyone of anything malicious back then. I trusted the system completely. I trusted my coworkers! I used to think the static on the two-way radio was just... static. Just old, outdated equipment in a city with way too many tall buildings bouncing the signals around. It never even crossed my mind that people could be using the interference to coordinate, or that they’d use coded language right out in the open like that. I was just so naive. I was just driving my bus, waving at the other drivers at the red lights, totally oblivious to what was actually going on under the surface. 

So, no, absolutely nothing like this before eight months ago. It wasn't until I was sitting in that glass office, actually looking at the raw data and hearing the unfiltered feeds, that the veil kind of lifted. And I think that's why it's so incredibly exhausting now, because it’s like I woke up in a completely different reality eight months ago. I can't go back to being that person who just thought static was static, because now I know the truth, but before that? No, my mind was totally clear.
Over these past eight months, have you felt emotionally flat or unable to feel much, even when things that used to matter to you happen?

Yeah, I mean, that’s exactly what I was trying to explain just a little bit ago when I was talking about the choir and the softball team. I know I already brought them up, but it really is the best way I can describe it, because it's not just that I stopped going... it's that I feel completely hollow about it. Like, flat. That's a really good word for it, actually. Flat. Because I used to feel this... this rush of joy, you know? When the Transit Titans would play, or when I was harmonizing with the altos on a Tuesday night. I felt alive. I felt connected to things. And now? It's like someone took the volume dial on my emotions and just cranked it all the way down to zero. 

When I told you about ignoring the choir director's texts... a year ago, I would have felt terrible! I would have been agonizing over it, feeling so guilty, texting him back right away with a million apologies because I cared so much about letting people down. But now, I look at the glowing screen on my phone and there is just... nothing. No guilt. No sadness. No missing the music or the people. It’s just a blank wall. 

And it’s the exact same thing when I’m sitting at that kitchen table every day after my shift. I mentioned how I just sit there with my planner open, right? Well, the worst part isn't even that I can't make myself start dinner or make those calls to the landlord or do anything else. The worst part is that I don't feel anything while I'm failing to do it. I'm not sitting
Have other people told you that your speech or the way you explain things has become hard to follow or disorganized?

Speech? Um... well, yeah, actually. A few of the drivers and the shift supervisor have made comments lately. They don't necessarily use the word "disorganized," they just... they act like I'm being intentionally difficult, you know? Which is so incredibly frustrating, because I'm really not. I'm just trying to keep everything together. 

Like, at work, in the dispatch office, we have this massive board. It's half digital now, but we still use the physical board with all these little colored magnets and paper route slips for the secondary buses and the detours. And lately, I just... I’ll get completely stuck rearranging them. The magnets and the slips, I mean. They have to be in this very specific, precise pattern. I’ll just stand there sliding them around, lining up the edges of the slips with the little blue magnets, making sure the alignments are absolutely perfect. Because if they aren't, it feels like the whole board is going to go wrong. Like the whole system will just collapse if the pattern isn't exactly right. 

And it's the same thing with how I talk on the radio now. When the drivers call in, I've started doing this thing where I have to repeat their last few words back to them before I can actually answer. Like, if a driver says he's "holding at the transit center," I have to say "transit center" back into the mic before I can give him his clearance or tell him his next time point. I just have to. It’s like I need to anchor the words so the route doesn't get messed up. 

But people just don't get it. They get so impatient with me. The supervisor will come in and ask me to explain why I'm taking so long on the radio, or why I'm moving the magnets around again instead of just logging the raw data, and when I try to explain it to them... when I try to tell them that I'm just trying to keep the whole board from going wrong... they just stare at me. They look at me like I'm speaking a completely different language. They'll sigh and say they can't follow what I'm talking about, or that I'm just making things complicated for no reason. They look at me like I’m just being difficult and stubborn, but I'm really, really not. I'm just trying to keep the grid safe, and they can't understand the way I'm explaining it.
Have you had the feeling that other people can hear your thoughts, as if your thoughts are being broadcast?

Hear my thoughts? Like... like they're playing over a loudspeaker or something? No. No, definitely not. Honestly, sometimes I wish they could, because if they could actually hear what was going on in my head, maybe they wouldn't look at me like I'm so difficult when I'm trying to explain the route alignments. If my thoughts were just broadcasting out into the dispatch office, then the shift supervisor—his name is Greg, he's been there for like fifteen years and thinks he knows absolutely everything—Greg would finally understand why the grid is so fragile right now. He'd hear my thoughts and say, "Oh, wow, she's actually right, we need to secure these time points." 

But no, they can't hear what I'm thinking. I know they can't because they're always so completely oblivious to it. When I'm sitting there in the glass office, watching the digital board and listening to the raw feeds, my mind is just racing, connecting all these dots about the tracking and the codes, and Greg will just walk by and ask if I want a stale donut from the breakroom. Just totally clueless. If he could hear my thoughts, he wouldn't be asking about pastries, you know? He'd be panicking right alongside me. 

So, no, my thoughts are... they're completely trapped in here. Which is honestly a relief, in a way, because with everything else going on, with the tracking and the radio static and feeling so exposed out in the open all the time... if they could get inside my head, too? I don't think I could handle that. The inside of my head is pretty much the only safe, private space I have left right now. Even if it is exhausting in there. So yeah, no, nothing like broadcasting. It's just the external stuff, the radios and the people watching, but my thoughts are just my own.
Have you been neglecting basic self-care, like showering or changing clothes?

Neglecting self-care? Like not showering? No. No, I mean... I still shower every single day. Actually, showering is one of the only things that still makes sense to me right now, because it's a routine I can just follow without having to make any big decisions. My alarm goes off at 4:45 AM, and I am in the shower by 4:50. I just have to be. I use this eucalyptus body wash because the smell kind of... it kind of clears my head before I have to go in and put the dispatch headset on. And the transit center, especially back in the offices, it has this really specific, heavy smell to it anyway—like a mix of diesel exhaust from the bays, burnt breakroom coffee, and whatever that industrial floor cleaner is they use on the linoleum. So I have to be clean before I go into that, and then when I get home, I usually shower again just to wash the whole day off my skin. 

And as for my clothes, I definitely change them. We have a uniform policy, so I wear these navy blue polos with the transit authority logo embroidered on the pocket, and either khaki or black slacks. I actually have exactly five of the polos, one for every day of my shift week, and I wash them all on Sunday and line them up in my closet. I make sure they're perfectly pressed, too. It’s just... it's part of keeping everything orderly, you know? If I show up to the dispatch office looking like a complete mess, how am I supposed to manage the grid? Greg, the supervisor I mentioned, he’s always coming in wearing these terribly wrinkled button-down shirts, and I just don't understand how he can expect to run a tight ship when he looks like he literally slept in his clothes. It bothers me so much to look at it. 

But for me? No, I always make sure I'm clean and put
For at least one full month, have these experiences of being tracked and hearing coded messages been present most days?

A month? Um, no, it has actually been longer than that. It has been... well, if I really look back at when it all started getting so undeniably obvious, it has been about two months now. Yeah, two solid months. Because I remember it started right around the time we did the quarterly route adjustments, which is always a massive headache anyway because they update the software on our dispatch terminals. And that is exactly when I started noticing the tracking through the computer system. 

At first, I thought maybe it was just a glitch with the new update, you know? Like maybe the GPS refresh rate was just lagging or the network was strained because everyone was logging in at once. But then it became an everyday thing. Literally every single day I sit down at my console, log into the transit grid, and I can just feel it. I can see the way the cursors move and the way the driver identification numbers blink on my screen, and it is not just raw data anymore. It is them tracking me. And
Have you done things lately that other people saw as very unusual or bizarre?

Unusual? Bizarre? I mean... I guess that depends entirely on who you ask, doesn't it? Because to me, it's not bizarre at all, it's completely necessary. But to other people—like Greg, or the drivers who just want to punch the clock and go home—yeah, I suppose they think I'm acting strange. 

Like, at work, in the dispatch office, we have this massive physical whiteboard that we use as a backup to the digital grid. It has all these little magnetic markers and route slips that correspond to the different bus lines and transit hubs. And lately... well, I have to arrange them. I'll get stuck there by the board, just rearranging the magnets and the slips in this very specific, very precise pattern. Because if they aren't lined up exactly right, the whole system feels off. It feels like the tracking is getting closer, like the grid is going to collapse. So I stand there, and I make sure the blue line magnets are perfectly parallel to the red line magnets, and the route slips are angled just so. And I know people are watching me. I can feel them staring at the back of my neck. I hear them whispering, wondering why I've been standing at the board for twenty minutes just adjusting pieces of plastic. 

And then there's the radio. When the drivers call in, they use these specific codes, right? And lately, before I can even key the mic to answer them, I find myself having to repeat their last few words back out loud. Just... echoing them. Like if a driver says, "Dispatch, this is 402, holding at the terminal," I have to say, out loud, to myself, "holding at the terminal," before I can press the button and say, "Copy that, 402." It's like I have to catch the words and process the code before I can respond, to make sure I'm not missing a hidden message or doing something that's going to trigger a route failure. 

And they hate it. The other dispatchers, the supervisors... they look at me like I'm just being difficult on purpose. Like I'm just trying to slow everything down or be an obstruction. Greg actually pulled me aside the other day and asked if I was "having trouble focusing." Focusing! I'm the only one who is actually focusing! They think it's just me being weird or bizarre, but they don't understand that I'm literally the only one trying to keep the whole board from going completely wrong. If I don't arrange the magnets, if I don't repeat the words to decipher the codes, the whole transit grid is going to fall apart, and they'll be the ones panicking. So, yeah, they think it's bizarre. But I'm just doing my job. I'm just trying to keep it all together.
Have you had the feeling that thoughts were being put into your mind by someone or something else?

Thoughts put into my mind? Like someone is forcing them in there? No. No, I haven't felt anything like that. I mean, my thoughts are definitely my own. They might be racing sometimes, especially when I'm at the console and trying to decipher all the codes coming over the radio, but they're still mine. I don't feel like someone is sitting in a control room somewhere beaming ideas into my head, if that's what you mean. 

It's actually the opposite, really. I feel like I'm the only one who is actually thinking clearly, the only one who sees what's really happening on the grid. Everyone else is just going through the motions, completely oblivious to the patterns. Like Greg, he just sits there drinking his burnt coffee and staring at the screen, and I know he's not really processing any of it. But my thoughts... they're sharp. They have to be, to keep up with the tracking and make sure the magnetic board is perfectly aligned. If I wasn't thinking my own thoughts, if I was just letting someone else dictate what I do, I'd probably be just as useless as the rest of them. So, no, nobody is putting thoughts into my mind. I'm just very, very focused on what I need to do.
Do you believe the people at work are trying to harm you in ways that could really happen in everyday life, rather than through supernatural or impossible means?

Harm me? Well... yes and no. I mean, they aren't trying to, like, physically attack me in the breakroom or poison my lunch or anything out of a movie. It's much more... bureaucratic than that, but it's just as real, and honestly, it's just as damaging. It's all about my job, my livelihood. 

I'm actually here, sitting in this office talking to you, because dispatch and the compliance department have been actively tracking every single one of my route changes. They do it right through the computer system. And it's not just the digital tracking, it's the radio, too. I hear these little comments, these specific phrases they use when they key the mic. It's like a coordinated effort to build a case against me. And I know what you're probably thinking, or what anyone else would say—they tell me it's just "normal oversight," just routine quality assurance, making sure the transit grid is running efficiently. That's the company line. 

But I can tell. I can absolutely tell that certain drivers are reporting on me directly. Like driver 714, for example. Every time he comes through the main hub, he pauses just a little too long near the dispatch window, and then later I'll see a flag on his route data that correlates exactly with a shift I was managing. They're trying to set me up to take the fall for when the grid inevitably has a massive failure. They want to fire me, or maybe even bring me up on some kind of gross negligence charges, which would completely ruin my life. So, yeah, it's very real, everyday harm they're planning. It's not magic, it's just corporate sabotage, and they're using the drivers and the software to do it.
For at least two weeks during this time, have you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Depressed? Like, sad and crying all the time? No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I don't think I've been depressed for two weeks straight, or really at all in the way you're probably meaning. It's not sadness that I'm feeling. It's more... well, it's just this intense, overwhelming pressure, you know? 

Because when you're the only one who actually sees the grid for what it is, when you're the only one keeping the route slips and the magnetic markers perfectly aligned so the whole system doesn't just collapse in on itself, there really isn't time to sit around and feel sad. I have to be on alert. I have to be watching the screens, listening to the radio codes, making sure driver 714 isn't lingering by the window again. If I were depressed, if I were just lying in bed all day with the curtains drawn, unable to get up, who would manage the board? Greg? Please. Greg can barely manage his own coffee order without messing it up. 

So, no, I haven't felt depressed most of the day. I'm exhausted, sure. I'm stressed out of my mind because of the tracking and the compliance department trying to build this ridiculous case against me. And it's incredibly frustrating, just deeply, deeply frustrating to be surrounded by people who think you're the problem when you're actually the solution. But that's not depression. That's just the reality of my situation at work right now. I'm just too focused on keeping everything from falling apart to be depressed.
Have you felt that some outside force was controlling your actions or movements?

Controlling my movements? Like a puppet on strings or something? No, no, definitely not. If anything, I have to have absolute, complete control over every single movement I make, down to the millimeter. 

When I'm standing at the magnetic board, you have to understand, it requires a very specific kind of physical precision. You can't just slap the route markers up there however you want. You have to slide them perfectly into the grid grooves, or the whole visual alignment gets thrown off for the next shift, and then you've got buses crossing paths in sector four. I mean, my hands are doing exactly what my brain tells them to do, and my brain is processing the grid. Sometimes my wrists actually ache by the end of a ten-hour shift from how tightly I have to grip the radio mic and how constantly I'm reaching and stretching to shift the heavy magnetic strips around on the upper tiers of the board. 

If some outside force was controlling my hands, I don't think I'd have these calluses on my fingers, you know? And honestly, if an outside force was controlling me, maybe they could do a better job of dealing with the compliance department, because I'm just exhausting myself trying to physically keep up with all the paperwork they keep generating. But no, every step I take across that dispatch floor, every time I reach up to adjust the frequency dial on the main console, every time I write down a timestamp... that's all me. It has to be me. Because if I let my guard down for even a second, if I wasn't in complete control of my own body and my own reactions, driver 714 would probably slip right past the window without me logging his exact entry time, and that's exactly what they want. So no, I'm the one moving my arms and legs. Nobody else is doing it for me.
Have the beliefs about being tracked at work only happened during times when you felt emotionally flat or unable to care about things?

Emotionally flat? Like I don't care about anything? Oh, definitely not. It's actually the exact opposite of that. I care so much, probably too much, honestly. Because if I didn't care, if I was just emotionally checked out, I wouldn't be paying such close attention to everything dispatch is doing.
